lead: A semiconductor laser diode is a forward-biased p-n junction that supplies its own light and its own mirrors. Cleaved crystal faces at the two ends form a Fabry–Perot cavity. Below a threshold current the diode behaves like an expensive LED; above it, stimulated emission wins and the output becomes narrow-band, directional and coherent. Every long-haul link, metro ring and FTTH feeder in India ends in one of these devices. Some syllabi call it an injection laser diode (ILD).
prereq: You need: 3.1 for stimulated emission, 3.2 for the forward-biased emitting junction, and 3.3 for population inversion, feedback and the threshold gain condition.

sections.h3: The diode is its own cavity

blocks.text: A laser diode is a p-n junction with a very thin active layer — tens of nanometres to about 0.1 µm — between two wider-bandgap cladding layers. Forward bias injects electrons from the n-side and holes from the p-side into that layer, and they recombine there. At low current the device emits spontaneous light exactly as the LED of 3.2 does.

Two things change the picture. The active layer is thin and the current density high, so carriers are injected faster than spontaneous recombination alone can remove them. The carrier density builds until the recombination rate matches the injection rate, and at that density population inversion exists between the bands — the condition from 3.3. And the crystal is cleaved along natural planes at both ends, leaving two flat parallel faces. The semiconductor index is near 3.5 and air is 1, so each face reflects a fraction R = ((n − 1)/(n + 1))² ≈ 0.30, where n is the refractive index.

Thirty per cent per facet is enough. Light travelling along the cavity is amplified by stimulated emission on each pass, reflects at a facet and comes back. Gain per pass must exceed loss per pass — mirror loss plus internal loss — and that is the threshold of 3.3.

sections.h3: Threshold, slope efficiency and the L-I curve

blocks.text: Written as a current density, the threshold condition in the linear-gain approximation is:

blocks.where: J_th is threshold current density in A/m² (device data sheets quote A/cm²); α_i is internal loss per metre; α_m = (1/2L)·ln(1/(R₁R₂)) is mirror loss per metre for cavity length L in metres and facet reflectivities R₁, R₂; Γ is the confinement factor, the fraction of the optical mode overlapping the active layer; β is gain per metre per A/m².

blocks.text: A double heterostructure confines both carriers and the optical field to the thin active layer. The carrier confinement raises the gain coefficient β and the heterobarriers keep α_i small, so J_th falls even though Γ is only a few tenths (typically 0.1–0.4 for a bulk active layer). Quantum wells go further (see 3.5).

A shorter cavity raises α_m and so raises J_th, but the active area shrinks, so the threshold current I_th = J_th × area falls. Lengthening the cavity lowers α_m and J_th, but raises I_th. Cavity length trades threshold current against mirror loss.
Above threshold the light-current curve is a straight line:

blocks.where: P is emitted optical power in W; I is forward current in A; I_th is threshold current in A; η_s is slope efficiency in W/A, and η_s = η_d (hν/q) with η_d the differential quantum efficiency (a pure number, at most 1), hν the photon energy in J and q = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

blocks.text: Typical values for a Fabry–Perot laser at 1.3–1.55 µm are I_th = 10–30 mA and η_s = 0.1–0.3 W/A. Subtract I_th, never I. Below threshold the idealised curve of the figure is zero; a real diode still shows a weak spontaneous tail of a few microwatts.
The cavity is a few hundred micrometres long, so many longitudinal modes fit inside the gain band. Their spacing is:

blocks.where: Δλ is mode spacing in m; λ is centre wavelength in m; n_g is group index, about 3.5–4; L is cavity length in m. For λ = 1.55 µm, n_g = 3.5, L = 300 µm, Δλ ≈ 1.14 nm.

blocks.text: Transverse modes are set by waveguide width and layer structure. A ridge a few micrometres wide supports one transverse mode, which is what a single-mode fiber needs; a broad stripe oscillates in several and is harder to couple (see 3.6).

blocks.where: T and T₀ are temperatures in kelvin and T_c is the characteristic temperature in kelvin. T_c is 50–70 K for InGaAsP devices near 1.3 µm and above 100 K for GaAs-based ones; a small T_c means the laser needs a cooler or a bias-tracking circuit.

blocks.text: Direct modulation adds the signal to the bias current. The diode must stay biased above threshold, otherwise every pulse starts with a turn-on delay. Carrier density and refractive index move together, so the wavelength chirps during each pulse, and that chirp turns into dispersion penalty in the fiber (see Unit 2, Chromatic dispersion). Directly modulated DFB lasers reach a few Gb/s; beyond that an external modulator is used (see 3.8).

figure.caption: Output power against current for a laser with a 20 mA threshold and a 0.30 W/A slope. The trace is flat at zero up to threshold, then straight: 40 mA gives 6 mW and 60 mA gives 12 mW.

spec.aria: Plot of laser output power against current: zero below 20 mA threshold, then a straight line with slope 0.3 mW per mA.

examples.question: A Fabry–Perot laser diode has threshold current 20 mA and slope efficiency 0.30 W/A. (a) Find the output optical power at 40 mA and at 60 mA. (b) At 60 mA the forward voltage is 1.8 V; find the electrical input power and the overall efficiency.
steps: Convert currents to amperes: I_th = 0.020 A, 40 mA = 0.040 A, 60 mA = 0.060 A.
Electrical input at 60 mA: P_elec = V·I = 1.8 × 0.060 = 0.108 W = 108 mW.
Overall efficiency: η = 12.0 mW / 108 mW = 0.111, i.e. 11.1%. Most of the input is heat, which is why a laser package sits on a heat sink.
examples.answer: 6.0 mW at 40 mA and 12.0 mW at 60 mA; at 60 mA the input is 108 mW and the overall efficiency is 11.1%.
examples.check:
i_th = 0.020
eta_s = 0.30
for i_ma in (40, 60):
    p = (i_ma/1000 - i_th) * eta_s
    print(round(p*1000, 3))
v = 1.8
i = 0.060
p_elec = v * i
print(round(p_elec*1000, 3))
print(round(12e-3/p_elec, 4))

traps: Using the whole current instead of (I − I_th): at 60 mA with η_s = 0.30 W/A you get 18 mW, not 12 mW.
Slope efficiency is a slope in W/A, not a percentage. The percentage is the differential quantum efficiency η_d, and the two differ by the factor hν/q.
Threshold current (mA) and threshold current density (A/cm²) are different quantities; J_th multiplied by active area gives I_th.
Longitudinal mode spacing comes from cavity length, transverse modes come from waveguide width. Examiners swap the two words.
Mirror loss α_m and internal loss α_i are separate terms that add inside J_th; a small R lowers reflectivity and raises threshold, it does not raise output.

quiz.q: Define slope efficiency and give its unit.
quiz.a: Slope efficiency η_s is the increase in output optical power per unit increase in current above threshold. Unit: W/A.

quiz.q: What fraction of light is reflected at an uncoated cleaved facet of a laser with n = 3.5?
Why does the L-I curve not rise from I = 0?
quiz.a: Below threshold the gain per pass is less than mirror plus internal loss, so stimulated emission cannot build up. Only spontaneous emission escapes, a few microwatts growing weakly with current. Above I_th the gain clamps at the loss value and extra current converts to coherent output.

quiz.q: Why does a double heterostructure lower the threshold current density?
quiz.a: It confines both carriers and the optical mode to a thin active layer. Carrier confinement greatly increases the gain β per unit current density and keeps the internal loss α_i small; Γ is only moderate (a few tenths) but the product Γβ still rises, so J_th = (α_i + α_m)/(Γβ) drops. The thin layer also shrinks the active volume, so the threshold current I_th falls further.

quiz.q: A laser has I_th = 25 mA and η_s = 0.25 W/A. Find the output at 55 mA.
A cavity is 300 µm long with group index 3.5, emitting at 1.3 µm. Find the longitudinal mode spacing.
A laser's threshold current doubles when the temperature rises by 30 K. Find its characteristic temperature.
quiz.a: I_th(T)/I_th(T₀) = exp(ΔT/T_c) = 2, so T_c = 30/ln 2 = 43.3 K. Such a low T_c means heavy temperature dependence and a need for cooling or bias tracking.

quiz.q: Why does direct modulation of a laser add dispersion penalty in a long link?
quiz.a: Modulating the current changes carrier density, which changes the refractive index and therefore the emitted wavelength. Each pulse is chirped, so its spectrum is wider than the dispersion limit allows; the fiber spreads the pulse and the receiver sees intersymbol interference.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production 1.55 µm transmitters replace the plain Fabry–Perot cavity with a distributed feedback (DFB) grating that selects one longitudinal mode, or use a vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser (VCSEL) for short data-centre links. Tunable lasers slide the grating electrically across the C-band for reconfigurable WDM networks (see Unit 6, WDM concepts). Silicon photonics puts lasers, modulators and waveguides on one chip. Search for 'DFB laser side-mode suppression ratio', 'VCSEL data link' and 'C-band tunable laser'.
